analysis.one_liner: Bans discrimination based on sex, race, national origin, sexual orientation, or disability in federally funded health care.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Rep. Laura Richardson with 2 cosponsors in December 2007, was referred to a House committee and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it illegal for any health care service or research program that gets federal money to discriminate against anyone because of sex, race, color, national origin, sexual orientation, or disability. That means a person could not be denied care, excluded from a program, or treated differently in medical research because of who they are. The bill was introduced late in 2007 and never moved past its first committee assignment.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients, medical research participants, and communities of color, women, people with disabilities, and LGBTQ people who rely on federally funded health care programs and research. If discrimination occurs, they would have a clear federal prohibition backing them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients in federally funded health programs

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits any health care service or research program receiving federal financial assistance from excluding, denying benefits to, or discriminating against a person on the basis of sex, race, color, national origin, sexual orientation, or disability status.
It extends an explicit federal nondiscrimination rule to sexual orientation in federally assisted health care, an area where such protections were not clearly established in law at the time.

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals, clinics, health care programs, and medical research institutions that receive federal funding would bear the cost of complying with the nondiscrimination rules, and could face legal claims if they discriminated.

drawbacks.text: Federally funded health care providers and research institutions would take on new compliance obligations and potential legal exposure under the nondiscrimination rule, costs that could add to their administrative burden.

The bill as introduced was a single short section; it did not spell out how the ban would be enforced, what remedies affected patients would have, or how agencies should apply it, leaving key questions to later interpretation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but largely duplicative of existing federal civil rights law in health care: race, color, national origin, sex, and disability discrimination in federally funded programs were already prohibited under earlier statutes, so the main new ground covered was sexual orientation. The cost to providers is modest compliance burden, but the bill's silence on enforcement made its practical effect hard to judge.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee in December 2007 and stayed there until the two-year Congress ended, never reaching a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Laura Richardson introduced the bill on December 19, 2007, in the final weeks of the first session of the 110th Congress, with 2 Democratic cosponsors.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce and then to the Subcommittee on Health.
No further action was taken, and the bill died when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one had to defeat the bill; it faded in committee with only three sponsors behind it. Federally funded health providers and research institutions avoided any new nondiscrimination compliance obligations, and the status quo in federal health civil rights enforcement continued unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo; providers faced no new rules

for.name: Rep. Laura Richardson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the House and assigned it to the Energy and Commerce Committee.

for.name: 2 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it a total of three supporters in the House.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of first referral, chaired by Rep. John Dingell (D-MI)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never acted on it; it sat in the committee and its Health Subcommittee for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so the partisan split was never tested; the sponsor and both cosponsors were Democrats.

industries.industry: Hospitals and health care providers receiving federal funds
industries.note: The bill would have imposed nondiscrimination obligations and potential legal exposure on any health care program taking federal money. Patients in those programs would have gained a clearer federal right to equal treatment, so the industry's cost was the public's gain.

Federally funded research programs would have been barred from excluding or treating participants differently based on the listed characteristics, adding compliance duties. Participants from minority, female, disabled, and LGBTQ communities would have gained protection.
